title: China Presses an End to 'Provocative Acts' at the Xiangshan Forum Ahead of Xi-Trump Summit as Congress Passes Sweeping Sanctions on Russia
subhead: Beijing used its premier security forum to set the tone before a looming Xi-Trump meeting while hardening its war-mobilization law, even as the U.S. Congress locked in a new round of sanctions on Russia and the Iran war entered an apparent endgame.

sections.heading: Xiangshan Forum and the Shadow of a Xi-Trump Summit
sections.body:
China's annual Xiangshan security forum opened with Defense Minister-level calls to end what Beijing calls 'provocative acts' in the region, an implicit rebuke of U.S. and allied patrols around Taiwan and the South China Sea, according to Reuters. The South China Morning Post reports the minister deliberately skirted the specific flashpoints, framing the tone-setting for a much larger event: a summit between Xi Jinping and President Trump. Taipei Times frames the same moment as Beijing 'seeking leverage before the US summit.'

The diplomatic choreography sits on top of a hard legal shift. Defense News reports China has changed its law to mobilize all national resources in the event of conflict, prompting allied questions about how close to a war footing Beijing is preparing to move. The combination of an outreach summit and an expanded mobilization statute is a signal that Beijing wants both a diplomatic off-ramp and a credible threat that its options are not limited to talks.
sections.whyItMatters: A Xi-Trump summit would be Beijing's best chance to reset the U.S.-China temperature, but it arrives alongside a domestic legal apparatus increasingly geared for all-out mobilization. The summit outcome, not the forum rhetoric, will determine whether the next phase is de-escalation or drift toward confrontation.

sections.heading: Iran War Enters an Apparent Endgame, With Houthis Still Escalating
sections.body:
President Trump said the U.S.-Iran war is 'toward the end' and claimed he has spoken directly with Tehran, while the House Speaker declared the Iranian nuclear issue 'taken care of,' as CBS News and Al Jazeera report. The Washington Post, however, argues Iran's leverage is 'dwindling' — a sign the administration believes its military pressure is now the dominant fact on the table.

The endgame narrative collides with continued fighting. Houthis claimed new attacks on a Saudi oil facility and an air base and seized two islands, per ABC News and Al Jazeera, prompting Saudi Arabia to warn of a 'red line' after a Houthi drone was downed near Makkah, according to The National. Washington says Saudi Arabia's east-west oil pipeline, targeted earlier, is set to resume — a concrete step toward restoring non-Hormuz export capacity even as Yemen fighting grinds on.
sections.whyItMatters: If Washington and Tehran are genuinely negotiating down the war while the Houthis widen the Saudi front, the trajectory splits: a Gulf de-escalation could be undone at any moment by a single Red Sea strike aimed at Saudi territory. The 'red line' language from Riyadh is the most volatile variable in the endgame.

sections.heading: Hormuz and the Oil Floor That Isn't Coming Down
sections.body:
Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has fallen to a new low, with NewsNation reporting the decline and Iran International adding that volumes plunged ahead of Iran-China talks. The CEPR released an analysis framing 2026 as a genuine 'Hormuz shock' for energy markets, while Standard Chartered sees a higher oil floor as the crisis spreads from the strait to Saudi export routes, according to OilPrice.com.

The strategic read is that oil markets have stopped pricing a quick return to normal. Even with direct U.S.-Iran contact reported, tanker underwriting, insurance and rerouting take months to unwind. The resumption of the Saudi east-west pipeline is a supply-side fix on the margin, but it does not resolve a choke point that markets now treat as persistently impaired.
sections.whyItMatters: A persistent Hormuz impairment — even at a de-escalated conflict level — keeps a war-risk premium baked into global energy prices and shipping costs. That is the economic channel through which the conflict affects every importer and every inflation forecast, independent of the military headlines.

sections.heading: Congress Locks In Sweeping Sanctions on Russia as the Drone War Grinds On
sections.body:
The U.S. Congress passed a sweeping sanctions bill targeting Russia, Al Jazeera reports, giving legislative teeth to what has largely been administered by executive order. It lands as the EU's top diplomat Kaja Kallas told the European Parliament there is an 'urgent need' for more EU support to Ukraine against Russia's escalation, per an EEAS statement.

On the ground, the war shows no sign of moderating. Russian drones killed five people on a bus and train in what the Independent described as 'an act of brutality,' while Ukraine reported eliminating a Russian general in occupied Donetsk, per the Kyiv Independent and The Guardian. Separately, Putin urged Russians to turn out for the parliamentary vote as a demonstration of support for the war, according to France 24, and Forbes flagged that both sides have escalated the energy war to a new stage.
sections.whyItMatters: Congressional sanctions harden the U.S. position into statute at the same time allies publicly warn of escalation and the frontline drone war intensifies. The diplomatic 'off-ramp' discussion that surfaced in earlier weeks has yielded, for now, to institutionalized pressure and continued fighting.

sections.heading: The Cost of the Iran War Is Reshaping U.S. Military Readiness
sections.body:
The Independent reports the Iran war has now cost some $33 billion, with the U.S. military facing weapons shortages after dozens of aircraft were destroyed. The Pentagon watchdog's confirmation of munitions shortfalls — flagged in Tuesday's brief — has become a recurring theme, and the Washington Post ties it to Iran's dwindling leverage: Washington's willingness to absorb high munitions and aircraft losses is itself a coercive signal to Tehran.

The strategic implication is twofold. Sustained attrition against Iran's air defenses and launch sites has depleted stocks that would be needed in any simultaneous contingency, particularly an Indo-Pacific one. And the sheer cost is beginning to shape domestic politics around the war's duration, even as the administration argues it is close to the finish line.
sections.whyItMatters: Readiness is the quiet constraint on U.S. strategy. A war that costs tens of billions and burns through precision munitions narrows Washington's options elsewhere in the world at exactly the moment it is trying to deter China and manage a broad set of crises simultaneously.

bottomLine: The day's clearest signal is a shift in tone on two fronts at once. Beijing went to its flagship security forum to pitch a summit while quietly hardening its mobilization law, and Washington coupled reported direct talks with Tehran to a Congress that just locked in new Russia sanctions and is absorbing a $33 billion war bill. The risk is that both superpowers are positioning for a diplomatic off-ramp they have not yet reached — Beijing and Washington ahead of a Xi-Trump summit, Washington and Tehran amid Houthi attacks that still threaten Saudi territory. Watch the two summits, not the headlines: whether either produces real commitments will define the next month.
